scenarios.title: The room that holds its temperature
scenarios.situation: A facilities team installs a heater that runs at full power whenever the room is below target and shuts off above target. The room swings between chilly and stifling, and the team blames the heater's wattage.
scenarios.prompt: What is actually wrong, in cybernetic terms?
evidence: Feedback

A negative feedback loop senses the output (temperature) and acts to reduce the deviation from the goal. The heater already implements one — the problem is not missing feedback but its crude form: full-on/full-off control with no modulation overshoots the target in both directions.
choices: The loop exists but is badly tuned: bang-bang control with no proportional response overshoots, so the fix is better control (e.g., proportional or PID control), not a bigger heater.
The system has positive feedback: the heater amplifies temperature errors, and the only fix is to remove the sensor.
The system has no feedback at all; a thermostat cannot work without a digital computer.
The wattage is simply too high; a smaller heater would hold temperature steady without any control changes.
scenarios.why: Negative feedback is present — the sensor does drive the heater. The failure is in the control law: on/off switching around the setpoint guarantees oscillation. Cybernetics distinguishes the loop's existence from its tuning.
scenarios.hint: Is the problem that feedback is missing, or that it is crude?

scenarios.title: Which way does the loop go?
scenarios.situation: During a market panic, falling prices frighten investors, who sell, which pushes prices lower. A commentator calls this 'the market's thermostat restoring balance.'
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the thermostat analogy?
choices: The loop is positive, not negative: falling prices cause more selling, which amplifies the fall — the opposite of a thermostat, which counteracts deviation. The commentator has the sign of the feedback backwards.
The analogy is correct: markets always return to equilibrium, exactly like a thermostat.
The analogy fails because markets have no sensors; feedback requires electronic measurement.
The analogy fails because thermostats cannot model human behavior under any circumstances.
scenarios.why: Sign matters more than the word 'feedback'. Negative feedback damps deviation toward a goal; positive feedback amplifies it away from the goal. Panics are runaway positive loops.
scenarios.hint: Does the effect oppose the cause, or reinforce it?

scenarios.title: The wobbling shower
scenarios.situation: An engineer models an office HVAC controller that reads the room sensor, but the sensor data arrives 10 minutes late. In simulation the temperature oscillates wildly even though the control law is a textbook negative-feedback design.
evidence: Delay destabilizes feedback

Wiener and the early control engineers learned that delay in a feedback loop turns correction into overcorrection: by the time the sensor reports 'too cold,' the heater has already been running too long. Sufficient delay makes even negative feedback oscillate or diverge.
choices: Sensor delay: the controller acts on stale information, so its corrections arrive out of phase and overshoot — a stable control law becomes oscillatory once the loop delay exceeds the system's response time.
The control law must be positive feedback in disguise; negative feedback can never oscillate.
The simulation timestep is too coarse; real hardware would not oscillate.
The sensor is miscalibrated; recalibration alone will remove the oscillation regardless of delay.
scenarios.why: Feedback acts on the past. When delay is large relative to how fast the system responds, yesterday's correction becomes today's overshoot. This is why control design starts with loop timing, not just the control law.
scenarios.hint: What does the controller know, and when does it know it?

scenarios.title: The regulator's variety
scenarios.situation: A data-center team builds an automated controller to keep 5,000 servers within thermal limits during heat waves, cold snaps, hardware failures, and traffic spikes. The controller handles exactly one scenario: 'it is hot outside.' The first cold snap crashes the cooling plant.
scenarios.prompt: Which cybernetic principle did the design violate?
evidence: Ashby's law of requisite variety

W. Ross Ashby's law states that a regulator must have at least as much variety (distinct responses) as the disturbances it regulates — 'only variety can destroy variety.' A one-response controller cannot regulate a many-disturbance environment.
choices: Requisite variety: the controller's repertoire (one response) is smaller than the disturbance set (heat, cold, failure, spikes), so unmodeled disturbances defeat it — the fix is widening the controller's variety, not tuning the single response.
The law of unintended consequences: automation always fails, so the plant should be run manually.
Occam's razor: the controller should be even simpler, with zero responses and a fixed schedule.
Moore's law: the controller needs faster hardware to handle the cold snap.
scenarios.why: Control is a matching problem: the regulator's variety must cover the environment's variety. Every disturbance you cannot respond to is a disturbance that controls you.
scenarios.hint: Count the disturbances, then count the responses. What must be true?

scenarios.title: The observer in the loop
scenarios.situation: A company evaluates its new AI support agent by having the agent's own training team write the test questions, run the evaluation, and publish the score. The score is excellent; customers disagree.
scenarios.prompt: What does second-order cybernetics say about this evaluation?
evidence: Second-order cybernetics

Heinz von Foerster and the later cyberneticians insisted the observer is part of the system: who measures, with what interests and instruments, shapes what is observed. An evaluation cannot be understood apart from the evaluator's position in the loop.
choices: The evaluation is compromised at the design level: the observers (the training team) are inside the system they measure, with an interest in a good score — second-order cybernetics requires accounting for the observer, e.g., independent evaluators and customer-grounded metrics.
The evaluation is fine; second-order cybernetics proves that self-evaluation is the most accurate method.
The problem is sample size; the same team running more questions would fix the disagreement.
Observer effects apply only to quantum physics, not to software evaluation.
scenarios.why: First-order cybernetics studies the observed system; second-order studies the observing system. When the measurer benefits from the measurement, the loop includes the incentive — design the evaluation for that.
scenarios.hint: Who is watching the watcher, and what do they gain?

scenarios.title: The cost of surprise
scenarios.situation: Two logging formats record the same events. Format A uses a fixed 8-bit code per event type; Format B uses short codes for common events and long codes for rare ones. A teammate claims Format A is 'more efficient because every code is the same size.'
scenarios.prompt: Which format is more efficient, and what principle decides it?
evidence: Shannon entropy (1948)

Claude Shannon's 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' defined information entropy: the average surprise of a message source. Optimal codes give frequent symbols short codes — the average length cannot go below the entropy, and variable-length coding approaches it. Uniform codes waste bits on predictable symbols.
choices: Format B: Shannon's source coding theorem shows the lower bound on average code length is the entropy of the source, achieved by assigning shorter codes to more probable events — fixed-length codes overpay for predictable events.
Format A: uniform codes are always optimal because they simplify decoding, regardless of event probabilities.
They are equally efficient: both record the same events, so information content is identical.
Format A: entropy measures disorder, and uniform codes minimize disorder.
scenarios.why: Efficiency is about the average, not the individual code: match code length to probability. That is the operational meaning of entropy — expected surprise — and the basis of all modern compression.
scenarios.hint: If some events are far more common, where should the bits go?

lessons.title: Cybernetics — Core concepts
concepts: A feedback loop is circular causality: the system's output is sensed and fed back to influence its input. Negative feedback counteracts deviation from a goal (a thermostat); positive feedback amplifies deviation (a panic, a microphone squeal). The sign of the loop, not the presence of feedback, determines stability.

Norbert Wiener named the field in Cybernetics (1948): 'control and communication in the animal and the machine.' His wartime work on anti-aircraft predictors — aiming at where a plane will be, not where it is — made prediction-plus-correction the core of control, with roots in WWI-era gun directors and servomechanisms.

Delay is the great destabilizer. A feedback loop acts on the past; when sensor or actuator delay is large relative to the system's speed, corrections arrive out of phase and a well-designed negative-feedback loop oscillates or diverges. Control design begins with loop timing.

Claude Shannon's 1948 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' gave cybernetics its measure: entropy as expected surprise, and the source coding theorem bounding how efficiently messages can be encoded. Communication and control became quantities to engineer, not metaphors.

W. Ross Ashby's law of requisite variety: a regulator needs at least as much variety — distinct states and responses — as the disturbances it must handle. Only variety destroys variety; an under-varied controller is controlled by its environment.

Second-order cybernetics (Heinz von Foerster, the Macy Conferences' later years) puts the observer inside the system: measurement, modeling, and evaluation are themselves loops with interests and blind spots. Designing a system includes designing how it is observed.

example.code:
python3 - <<'EOF'
# Negative feedback with delay: thermostat simulation
temp, target, delay = 15.0, 20.0, 0
readings = [temp]*12
for t in range(60):
    sensed = readings[-(delay+1)]          # stale sensor
    power = max(0, (target - sensed)) * 0.8 # proportional control
    temp += power*0.15 - 0.10               # heat in, loss out
    readings.append(temp)
print(f"delay={delay}: final={temp:.1f}")
# re-run with delay=8 to watch oscillation appear
EOF
example.walkthrough: A proportional controller drives the room toward the target using sensed temperature. With delay=0 it settles; raise the delay and watch stable control turn oscillatory — the loop's timing, not its logic, is what breaks.

pitfalls: Common trap: saying 'feedback' when you mean 'negative feedback' — positive feedback is feedback too, and it destabilizes rather than regulates.
Common trap: tuning the control law while ignoring loop delay — no gain setting fixes a sensor that reports the past as the present.
Common trap: treating Shannon entropy as 'disorder' in the colloquial sense — in the theory it is expected surprise, a precise bound on encodability.
Common trap: building a regulator with less variety than its environment, then blaming the one disturbance it was never designed to meet — Ashby's law is a design budget, not a suggestion.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Tune a thermostat, break a thermostat
labs.objective: Simulate a negative-feedback temperature controller and discover experimentally how sensor delay destroys stability.
steps: Copy the lesson's thermostat simulation into a file thermo.py.
Run it with delay=0 and record the final temperature — confirm it settles near the 20.0 target.
Re-run with delay=4, then delay=8, printing the last 10 readings each time; note when oscillation appears.
Add a bang-bang variant (full power below target, zero above) at delay=0 and compare its swing to proportional control.
Write two sentences: in a real deployment, what would you measure first — the control law or the loop delay? Why?

checks.hint: Print the delay value and final temperature on one line so the check can see the experiment ran.

labs.title: Measure the surprise
labs.objective: Compute Shannon entropy of a message source and build an optimal-ish variable-length code, proving Format B beats Format A.
steps: Define a source with four event types and probabilities, e.g., A=0.5, B=0.25, C=0.125, D=0.125.
Compute the entropy H = -sum(p * log2(p)) and the fixed-length cost (2 bits per event).
Assign codes by hand (A=0, B=10, C=110, D=111) and compute the average code length.
Verify your average length sits between the entropy and the fixed-length cost.
State in one line what the entropy value means operationally for this source.

checks.hint: Print the computed entropy with the word 'entropy' so the check can confirm the calculation ran.

simulations.title: The autoscaler that fed on its own alerts
simulations.brief: At 03:00 the fleet scaled from 12 to 400 instances, then collapsed. The scaling signal came from the monitoring the scaler itself was saturating. Diagnose the loop.

steps.symptom: 03:00 scale-up triggered by p99 latency alert. Each new instance increased monitoring load, which raised reported latency, which triggered more scale-up.
options: Runaway positive feedback: the controller's actions amplified the sensor reading that drove the controller
A DDoS attack
Bad deploy at 03:00
The monitoring agent has a memory leak
evidence: metrics.txt
03:00 p99=900ms (12 instances) -> 03:20 p99=2400ms (180 instances) -> 03:40 fleet 400, API down. Monitoring scrape load per instance: constant. Total scrape load grew 33x.
scaler-config.txt
Scale rule: IF p99 > 800ms THEN add 20%. Cooldown: 0s. No damping, no max cap.
steps.explain: This is circular causality in production: the effector (new instances) fed the sensor (latency, inflated by scrape load), which re-triggered the controller. Wiener's warning made concrete — a control loop with no damping and a corrupted sensor diverges.

steps.symptom: Positive feedback confirmed. What breaks the loop?
options: Add more instances faster
Introduce negative feedback: cooldown periods, a max instance cap, damping on the scale signal, and a sensor that measures real user latency instead of scrape-loaded latency
Disable the autoscaler permanently
Increase the latency threshold to 5000ms
evidence: control-theory.txt
Stability requires negative feedback: the correction must oppose the error, with delay and gain tuned so the loop converges instead of oscillating or diverging.
steps.explain: You do not fix a control loop by pushing harder — you fix it by making the feedback negative and honest: cooldowns and caps bound the gain, and an uncorrupted sensor closes the loop on reality.

simulations.debrief: Every autoscaler, alert pipeline, and incident response is a control loop. Ask of each one: what is the sensor, what is the effector, is the feedback negative, and what happens at the extremes. Positive feedback always finds the extreme.

simulations.title: Design the detection-response feedback loop
simulations.brief: You are designing the SOC's core loop: detection -> triage -> containment -> learning. The CISO asks where automation belongs and where humans belong. Decide the control architecture.

steps.symptom: Proposal A: full automation — detect, isolate, remediate, close, no humans. Proposal B: your design.
options: Proposal A — speed wins, humans are the bottleneck
A layered loop: fast inner loop (automated containment on high-confidence, reversible actions) inside a slow outer loop (human review, rule tuning, lessons learned feeding back into detection)
No automation — analysts handle everything
Automate only the ticketing
evidence: incident-review.txt
Last quarter: 2 false-positive auto-isolations took down payroll. 1 slow human triage let ransomware dwell 6 hours. Both failure modes are loop-design failures.
wiener-note.txt
Control without communication fails; communication without control is noise. The loop needs both machine speed and human judgment, each where it belongs.
steps.explain: Cybernetics gives the answer structure: nested loops at different timescales. The fast loop handles what is reversible and high-confidence; the slow loop — humans — handles judgment, novelty, and tuning the fast loop itself. Either extreme fails exactly as the incident review shows.

steps.symptom: The layered loop is approved. Where does the learning feedback go — what does the outer loop actually change?
options: It writes the incident report
It tunes the inner loop: detection thresholds, containment playbooks, confidence scores — every incident updates the controller's parameters
It hires more analysts
It buys more tools
evidence: soc-metrics.txt
MTTR fell 40% after the outer loop started feeding false-positive analysis back into rule tuning. Same tools, better controller.
steps.explain: The outer loop's product is a better inner loop. An incident that does not change a threshold, a playbook, or a score is information that never became control — entropy the organization paid for and threw away.

simulations.debrief: A SOC is a control system regulating the organization's risk state. Design it as nested feedback loops: fast automated inner loops for the reversible and certain, slow human outer loops for judgment — and every incident must tune the machine.

simulations.title: The deploy pipeline that could not decide
simulations.brief: The canary deployer has rolled forward and back six times in an hour. Each rollback triggers a redeploy, each redeploy triggers a rollback. Find the oscillation source.

steps.symptom: 18:00 deploy v2.4 -> 18:07 rollback (error budget) -> 18:12 redeploy (metrics recovered) -> 18:19 rollback... six cycles. Error rate hovers exactly at the threshold.
options: Hunting oscillation from delayed feedback: the health sensor lags reality, so the controller corrects for a state that no longer exists
The new version is simply broken
The old version is simply broken
Two engineers fighting over the deploy button
evidence: deployer.log
18:07 rollback decision used metrics from 17:52 (15-min aggregation lag). 18:12 redeploy used metrics from 18:00 (pre-rollback window). Each decision corrected the previous window's state.
metrics-raw.txt
Actual error rate: stable 0.8%, under the 1% threshold, the entire hour. The controller never saw the present.
steps.explain: Delayed feedback turns negative feedback into oscillation: by the time the sensor reports, the system has moved on, so every correction overshoots. The error rate was fine — the controller was steering by a stale map.

steps.symptom: Stale sensor confirmed. What stabilizes the loop?
options: Deploy faster to outrun the lag
Faster sensing plus hysteresis: shorten the aggregation window, and require the signal to clear the threshold by a margin for a sustained period before reversing a decision
Remove the error-budget gate
Increase the rollback threshold
evidence: control-theory.txt
Two cures for delay-induced oscillation: reduce the delay (faster sensor), and add hysteresis/deadband so the controller does not reverse on noise.
steps.explain: Hysteresis is the thermostat principle: the heater does not flip at exactly 20.0 degrees or it chatters forever. A margin plus a dwell time lets the loop settle instead of hunting.

simulations.debrief: Oscillation is the signature of feedback delay. When a system hunts — flapping between states — check the sensor's freshness before blaming the thing being controlled. Faster truth plus hysteresis calms the loop.

simulations.title: The SOC drowned in its own signals
simulations.brief: Alert volume tripled after a new log source came online: 12,000 alerts/day, 3 analysts. True positives are being missed in the flood. The channel is over capacity. Respond.

steps.symptom: 12,000 alerts/day. Analyst capacity: ~150 investigations/day. Missed: a real credential-stuffing campaign buried at position 9,400.
options: Hire 80 analysts
Treat it as a channel-capacity problem: the signal rate exceeds the receiver's bandwidth, so compress before transmitting — aggregate, deduplicate, prioritize, suppress the known-benign
Turn off the new log source
Tell analysts to work faster
evidence: alert-stats.txt
Of 12,000 daily alerts: 61% duplicates, 22% known-benign (tuned but not suppressed), 9% informational, 8% actionable. Effective signal: ~960/day.
shannon-note.txt
Information theory: a channel has finite capacity. When the source exceeds it, you encode smarter (compression, prioritization) — you cannot will the channel wider.
steps.explain: Shannon's answer applies to SOCs: the analysts are a finite-capacity channel. 92% of the volume is redundancy and noise — compress it out before it reaches the human, and the real signal fits the channel.

steps.symptom: Compression plan approved. What is the correct order of operations?
options: Suppress everything and tune later
Deduplicate first (safe, mechanical), then suppress the known-benign with documented rules, then risk-prioritize the remainder — measuring miss rate at each step
Prioritize first, dedupe later
Buy a bigger SIEM
evidence: rollout.txt
Dedup: -61% volume, zero miss risk. Known-benign suppression: -22%, each rule peer-reviewed. Prioritization: ranked queue, miss rate monitored weekly.
steps.explain: Order by reversibility and risk: mechanical dedup cannot hide signal, documented suppression is auditable, and prioritization keeps the residual risk visible and measured instead of silent.

simulations.debrief: Alert fatigue is an information-theoretic failure, not a morale failure. The fix is encoding: compress redundancy, filter the known-benign, prioritize the rest — and measure what the channel carries, not just its volume.

simulations.title: Hold the line: homeostasis under attack
simulations.brief: A traffic flood is pushing the API toward its breaking point. You must hold service levels steady — homeostasis — while the attack continues. Choose the control strategy.

steps.symptom: Traffic 8x normal, 70% from 200 source IPs with bot signatures. p99 latency climbing, error rate 2% and rising. SLO: 99.9% success.
options: Overprovision: spin up 10x capacity and absorb it
Negative-feedback control: rate-limit the abusive sources, shed low-priority load, serve degraded-but-correct responses — regulate the internal state against the disturbance
Shut down the API until the attack ends
Block the entire internet except allowlisted customers
evidence: capacity.txt
10x overprovisioning: 40 min to provision, cost 12x, and the botnet can scale faster than we can buy.
physio-note.txt
Homeostasis: the organism does not grow ten hearts under stress — it constricts vessels, prioritizes the brain, sheds heat. Regulate, don't just absorb.
steps.explain: Absorption loses to any attacker who can scale; shutdown surrenders. Homeostatic control — sense the disturbance, oppose it proportionally, protect the essential functions — holds the SLO while the storm passes.

steps.symptom: Rate limiting is holding the SLO. The attack shifts: now low-and-slow from 50,000 residential IPs. Your controller's move?
options: Give up — it cannot be rate-limited by IP anymore
Adapt the controller: shift from IP-based to behavior-based signals (request patterns, TLS fingerprints, challenge-response), keeping the same homeostatic goal
Block all residential IPs
Raise the rate limits so legitimate users are unaffected
evidence: adaptation.txt
Second-order control: when the disturbance changes form, the controller must change its sensor, not its goal. Goal (SLO) is invariant; the means adapt.
steps.explain: This is the cybernetic lesson in one move: the goal stays fixed while the control strategy adapts to the disturbance. Rigid controllers break; adaptive controllers hold.

simulations.debrief: Homeostasis is the original control problem: hold the essential variable steady while the environment rages. Sense honestly, oppose proportionally, and when the attack changes shape, change the sensor — never the goal.

consoleSims.title: Tune the controller setpoint
consoleSims.brief: In the autoscaler control panel, set the scale-up cooldown to 300 seconds to add damping to the loop, then submit.

tasks.hint: Click submit on the configuration form.

consoleSims.debrief: Cooldown is damping made concrete: a pause between corrections so the loop can observe the effect of the last one before issuing the next.

consoleSims.title: Open the oscillation incident
consoleSims.brief: Open a P2 ticket for the deploy-pipeline oscillation, assign it to the platform on-call, and move it to in-progress.

tasks.instruction: Create a P2 ticket titled 'Deploy pipeline oscillation — 6 flap cycles'.
tasks.hint: Create a P2 ticket titled 'Deploy pipeline oscillation — 6 flap cycles'.

consoleSims.debrief: Oscillation is an incident like any other: ticketed, owned, and worked until the loop is stable.

consoleSims.title: Damp the flood at the edge
consoleSims.brief: The botnet's primary source 198.51.100.23 is hammering the API. Drop its traffic on INPUT, then set the INPUT default policy to DROP.

tasks.instruction: Add a rule dropping all TCP traffic from 198.51.100.23 on INPUT (port 443).
tasks.hint: Add an INPUT rule: protocol tcp, port 443, source 198.51.100.23, action DROP.

tasks.instruction: Set the INPUT chain default policy to DROP.
tasks.hint: Set the default policy of the INPUT chain to DROP.

consoleSims.debrief: Edge filtering is the outermost control loop: oppose the disturbance as far from the core as possible, default-deny the rest.

consoleSims.title: Build the oscillation detector
consoleSims.brief: Create a SIEM rule that fires when any host flaps state more than 5 times in 10 minutes, then acknowledge the existing alert ALT-4100.

tasks.instruction: Create a detection rule named 'oscillation-flap' with query 'flap_count > 5'.
tasks.hint: Create a rule named oscillation-flap with query 'flap_count > 5'.

consoleSims.debrief: Detecting oscillation is itself a feedback loop: the sensor watches the controllers, and its output tunes them. Control all the way up.

terminalMissions.success_message: Telemetry format confirmed — the sensor feed is live.

terminalMissions.success_message: Latest readings captured — the controller is seeing fresh data.

terminalMissions.title: Sort the latency readings
terminalMissions.brief: Sort the latency readings to find the extremes the controller reacted to.
terminalMissions.success_message: Readings sorted — the spike that triggered scale-up is visible.

terminalMissions.title: Find controller errors
terminalMissions.brief: Search the controller log for ERROR lines around the incident window.
terminalMissions.success_message: Controller errors isolated — the decision points are mapped.

terminalMissions.title: Diff the controller configs
terminalMissions.brief: Compare the stable controller config against the one deployed before the incident.
terminalMissions.success_message: Config drift found — the removed cooldown explains the runaway.

terminalMissions.title: Count the telemetry samples
terminalMissions.brief: Count how many telemetry samples the sensor recorded during the incident.

terminalMissions.success_message: Sample count captured — the observation window is quantified.

terminalMissions.title: Echo the current setpoint
terminalMissions.brief: Print the controller's current setpoint value to confirm what the loop is regulating toward.
terminalMissions.success_message: Setpoint confirmed — the loop's target is explicit.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.

media.title: Indirect prompt injection attack flow
media.caption: An attacker hides instructions in data the agent retrieves; the agent mistakes data for instructions and misuses its tools.
media.alt: Attack flow diagram: hidden instruction in an email is read by an AI agent, which mistakes it for a command and calls a privileged tool, causing fraud; three defense boxes below: sanitize content, least-privilege tools, human approval.
